nameStory: The 'whiskered' part of this lichen's name comes from the tiny hair-like structures called cilia that fringe its edges, making it look like it's sporting delicate whiskers. The 'shadow' refers to its preference for growing in partially shaded spots rather than full sun, where many of its relatives thrive.
description: Whiskered Shadow Lichen is a crusty, gray-green lichen that forms small rosettes on tree bark and rocks. It grows in circular patches that rarely exceed an inch across, with lobes that radiate outward like petals on a flower. The surface has a somewhat powdery appearance and feels slightly rough to the touch. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae working as partners.

idTips.label: Whisker-like edge hairs
idTips.description: Look closely at the edges of the lobes with a hand lens - you'll see tiny white hair-like projections called cilia that give this species its distinctive 'whiskered' appearance

idTips.label: Gray-green color
idTips.description: The thallus (lichen body) is typically gray-green to pale greenish-gray, sometimes with a slightly bluish tint when moist

idTips.label: Small rosette form
idTips.description: Forms tight, circular rosettes usually less than an inch across, with narrow lobes radiating from the center like spokes on a wheel

idTips.label: Powdery surface texture
idTips.description: The surface feels slightly gritty or powdery when gently rubbed with a finger, and may appear somewhat frosted or dusty

idTips.label: Dark lower surface
idTips.description: If you can carefully lift an edge, the underside is typically dark brown to black with simple root-like structures called rhizines

habitat: This rare lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like maples and ashes in partially shaded locations. In New England, look for it in mixed hardwood forests at low to moderate elevations, often in areas with good air quality. It tends to prefer spots that get morning sun but afternoon shade, avoiding both deep forest shade and full exposure.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as it absorbs moisture from spring rains, taking on a greener hue. This is an excellent time to spot the distinctive whisker-like cilia along the edges.
seasonality.summer: May appear more gray and contracted during dry spells, but the characteristic rosette pattern and edge hairs remain visible. Look for it during humid mornings when it's more hydrated.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as deciduous trees lose their leaves, allowing more light to reach the bark. The lichen may show renewed growth activity during this season's consistent moisture.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round on bark, though it may appear more gray and dormant. Snow-free periods with good light are ideal for examination with a hand lens.

funFact: Despite being called 'whiskered,' those tiny hair-like structures along its edges aren't actually hairs at all - they're specialized fungal threads that help the lichen sense humidity levels and may even help it 'taste' the chemical composition of potential growing surfaces!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small gray lichens on bark, but the combination of its small rosette form and distinctive marginal cilia (whiskers) visible with a hand lens makes it unique. Memory trick: 'Whiskers on the edges, not the middle' - unlike some lichens that have fuzzy centers, this one keeps its 'facial hair' around the rim.
contextualKnowledge: This lichen is extremely rare in New England with only one documented observation, making any sighting scientifically valuable. The genus name Phaeophyscia comes from Greek words meaning 'dusky bubble,' referring to the inflated appearance of the fruiting bodies when present.
compareHints: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Whiskered Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its particularly prominent marginal cilia and small size. The closely related Ciliate Wreath Lichen is larger and has different surface chemistry, while the Hairy Shadow Lichen has hairs scattered across the surface rather than just at the edges. Most other shadow lichens in the genus lack the distinctive whisker-like edge hairs entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its bright orange pycnidial contents - most other wreath lichens in this genus have white, yellow, or red cores instead.
Among the shadow lichens in its genus, Pom-pom Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its small size and abundant powdery soredia clusters.
Among its wreath lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen is distinguished by having the white soredia concentrated specifically at the lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Ciliate Wreath Lichen is the only one with prominent white hair-like projections along all lobe edges.
Among its relatives, Hairy Shadow Lichen is distinguished by those characteristic hair-like edge projections that other shadow lichens lack.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Dark Shadow Lichen is easily recognized by its abundant black isidia that cover both the center and edges of the lobes.

Unlike its relatives such as Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange inner tissues) or Hairy Shadow Lichen (which has fuzzy edges), Mealy Shadow Lichen lacks both colorful internal tissues and hairy margins.

Unlike its relatives like Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange interiors) or Mealy Shadow Lichen (which has white powdery surfaces), Red-cored Starburst Shadow Lichen is the only species in its genus with the distinctive crimson interior.
Among its shadow lichen relatives, Scaly Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its prominently curled, squarrose lobes that create a three-dimensional texture.
